source_text: οὐκ ἦν μετ' αὐτῶν θεὸς ἀλ λότριος». 19.15 καὶ ὁ Ἱερεμίας ὡσαύτως· «καὶ οὐκ εἴπατε», φησίν, «ποῦ ἔστιν κύριος ὁ ἀναγαγὼν ὑμᾶς ἐκ γῆς Αἰγύπ του, ὁ καθοδηγήσας ὑμᾶς ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ;» 19.16 Ὁ δέ γε Ἠσαΐας τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα ὡδηγηκέναι λέγει· «ἤγαγεν γάρ», φησίν, «αὐτοὺς διὰ ἀβύσσου ὡς ἵππον δι' ἐρήμου καὶ οὐκ ἐκοπίασαν, καὶ ὡς κτήνη διὰ πεδίου κατέβη πνεῦμα παρὰ κυρίου καὶ ὡδήγη σεν αὐτούς». 19.17 Ὁ δὲ Παῦλος ὁδηγὸν αὐτῶν τὸν Χριστὸν γεγενῆσθαι διδάσκει· «ἔπινον γάρ», φησίν, «ἐκ πνευματικῆς ἀκολουθούσης πέτρας, ἡ δὲ πέτρα ἦν ὁ Χριστός». 19.18 ᾧ συνῳδὰ καὶ Ἰούδας καθολικῶς γράφει· «ἅπαξ γὰρ κύριος Ἰησοῦς λαὸν ἐξ Αἰγύπτου σώσας, δεύτερον τοὺς μὴ πισ τεύσαντας αὐτῷ ἀπώλεσεν». 19.19 Ἐνταῦθα οὖν διπλῶς ἀναιρεῖται ἡ ἐπιχείρησις τῶν λεγόντων κτίσμα τὸν σεπτὸν υἱὸν καὶ τὸ θεϊκὸν πνεῦμα, ἀπό τε τοῦ περὶ ἑκατέρας ὑποστάσεως κεχρησμῳδῆσθαι τὰ τὴν ἄπειρον μίαν φύσιν κατασημαίνοντα, ἀπό τε τοῦ παρακεῖσθαι ὅτι «οὐκ ἦν μετ' αὐτῶν θεὸς ἀλλότριος», τοῦτ' ἔστιν ἑτεροούσιος. 19.20 Τὸν ἴσον τρόπον Μωϋσῆς μὲν λέγει· «οὐκ ἔσται μερὶς οὐδὲ κλῆρος τοῖς Λευίταις ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς· κύριος αὐτὸς μερὶς αὐτῶν». Ἱερεμίας δέ· «ὁ πλάσας», φησίν, «τὰ πάντα αὐτὸς κληρονομία τοῦ Ἰακώβ. κύριος ὄνομα αὐτῷ». ∆αυῒδ δὲ ἐν ιεʹ ψαλμῷ· «κύριος μερὶς τῆς κληρονομίας μου καὶ τοῦ ποτηρίου μου». 19.21 Ὁ δέ γε Παῦλος τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα τὴν κληρονομίαν εἶναι Ἐφεσίοις ἐπιστέλλει· «ἐν ᾧ», φησίν, «πιστεύσαντες ἐσφραγίσθημεν τῷ πνεύματι τῆς ἐπαγγελίας τῷ ἁγίῳ, ὅ ἐστιν ἀρραβὼν τῆς κληρονομίας ἡμῶν». 19.22 ὁμοίως Παῦλος Κορινθίοις γράφει· «διαιρέσεις δὲ χαρισμάτων εἰσίν, τὸ δὲ αὐτὸ πνεῦμα· καὶ διαιρέσεις διακονι ῶν εἰσιν, καὶ ὁ αὐτὸς κύριος· καὶ διαιρέσεις ἐνεργημάτων εἰσιν, ὁ δὲ αὐτὸς θεὸς ὁ ἐνεργῶν τὰ πάντα ἐν πᾶσιν». 19.23 δεικνὺς δὲ τὴν ταυτότητα τῆς θεότητος οὐ μόνον ἐνταῦθα πρώτου ἐπιμέμνηται τοῦ πνεύματος, εἶτα τοῦ υἱοῦ καὶ οὕτω τοῦ πατρός, ἀλλὰ καὶ ὁ νῦν εἰρηκὼς τὸν θεὸν τὰ πάντα ἐνεργεῖν, μετ' ὀλίγον ἐπάγει· «ταῦτα δὲ πάντα ἐνεργεῖ τὸ ἓν καὶ τὸ αὐτὸ πνεῦμα διαιροῦν ἰδίᾳ ἑκάστῳ, καθὼς βούλεται», 19.24 σαφῶς καὶ διαρρήδην αὐτὸ θεὸν ὁμοούσιον τῷ πατρὶ καὶ τῷ υἱῷ ἅμα καὶ αὐτεξούσιον παριστῶν. 19.25 Ἔστιν ἀκοῦσαι καὶ τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ πατρὸς παρ' Ἠσαΐᾳ μὲν εἰρηκότος·
pass_a_gloss: [...] there was not with them a foreign god.' 19.15 And Jeremiah in the same way: 'and you did not say', he says, 'where is the Lord who led you up out of the land of Egypt, who guided you down through the wilderness?' 19.16 But Isaiah says the Holy Spirit has guided [them]: 'for he led them', he says, 'through the abyss like a horse through a desert, and they did not grow weary, and like beasts through a plain, a spirit came down from the Lord and guided them.' 19.17 But Paul teaches that Christ became their guide: 'for they were drinking', he says, 'from a spiritual following rock, and the rock was the Christ.' 19.18 In accord with which Jude also writes catholically (in his catholic letter): 'for once the Lord Jesus, having saved a people out of Egypt, the second time destroyed those not having believed in him.' 19.19 Here then doubly is destroyed the attempt of those saying [are] a creature the venerable Son and the divine Spirit, both from the things signifying the infinite one nature having been oracled about each hypostasis, and from its lying alongside that 'there was not with them a foreign god', that is, of another substance. 19.20 In the equal manner Moses says: 'there will not be a portion nor a lot to the Levites upon the land; the Lord himself is their portion.' And Jeremiah: 'the one having formed', he says, 'all things is himself the inheritance of Jacob. Lord is name to him.' And David in psalm 15 (LXX; English 16): 'the Lord is portion of my inheritance and of my cup.' 19.21 But Paul writes to Ephesians that the Holy Spirit is the inheritance: 'in whom', he says, 'having believed we were sealed with the Spirit of the promise, the holy one, which is pledge of our inheritance.' 19.22 Likewise Paul writes to Corinthians: 'and there are distributions of gifts, but the same Spirit; and there are distributions of ministries, and the same Lord; and there are distributions of workings, but the same God, the one working all things in all.' 19.23 And showing the sameness of the Godhead, not only does he here first make mention of the Spirit, then of the Son, and thus of the Father, but also the one who has just said that God works all things, after a little brings on: 'and all these things the one and the same Spirit works, distributing individually to each, just as he wills', 19.24 clearly and expressly presenting it as God of the same substance with the Father and the Son, and at once self-determining. 19.25 It is possible to hear also God and Father, having said, in Isaiah on the one hand: [...]
pass_b_english: … there was no foreign god with them” (Deuteronomy 32:12). And Jeremiah likewise: “And you did not say,” he says, “Where is the Lord who brought you up out of the land of Egypt, who guided you in the wilderness?” (Jeremiah 2:6).

But Isaiah says that it was the Holy Spirit who guided them: “For he led them through the deep,” he says, “like a horse through the desert, and they did not grow weary; and like cattle through a plain, the Spirit came down from the Lord and guided them” (Isaiah 63:13-14).

And Paul teaches that Christ became their guide: “For they drank,” he says, “from a spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4). In harmony with him Jude too writes in his catholic letter: “For the Lord Jesus, having once saved a people out of Egypt, afterward destroyed those who did not believe in him” (Jude 1:5).

Here, then, the argument of those who call the venerable Son and the divine Spirit a creature is overthrown twice over: first, because the words that signify the one infinite nature have been spoken in prophecy of each hypostasis; and second, because beside them stands the line “there was no foreign god with them,” that is, none of another substance.

In the same way Moses says: “The Levites shall have no portion or lot in the land; the Lord himself is their portion” (Deuteronomy 18:1-2; Numbers 18:20). And Jeremiah: “He who formed all things,” he says, “is himself the inheritance of Jacob; the Lord is his name” (Jeremiah 10:16). And David in the sixteenth Psalm: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance and of my cup” (Psalm 16:5).

But Paul, writing to the Ephesians, says that the Holy Spirit is the inheritance: “In whom,” he says, “having believed, we were sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise, who is the pledge of our inheritance” (Ephesians 1:13-14). Likewise Paul writes to the Corinthians: “Now there are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit; and there are varieties of ministries, and the same Lord; and there are varieties of workings, but it is the same God who works all things in all” (1 Corinthians 12:4-6).

And to show the identity of the Godhead, he not only names the Spirit first here, then the Son, and only then the Father; but he who has just said that God works all things adds a little later: “But all these things are worked by one and the same Spirit, who distributes to each one individually as he wills” (1 Corinthians 12:11). So he presents the Spirit clearly and in so many words as God, of one substance with the Father and the Son, and at the same time as free and sovereign in his own right.

choices.issue: Old draft garbled, with wrong Psalm number and ranges
choices.choice: Retranslated the whole section from the Greek. The old English made 19.19 say 'the seventh Son' (σεπτόν is 'venerable'), invented 'the use of another hypostasis as a pretext', and lost Didymus' two grounds (the same divine words spoken of each hypostasis; 'no foreign god', that is, none of another substance); rendered οὐκ ἦν μετ' αὐτῶν θεὸς ἀλλότριος 'God was not a stranger among them'; made καθολικῶς 'universally'; and called the Greek ψαλμὸς ιεʹ 'the 14th Psalm' (it is Psalm 15 in Greek numbering, Psalm 16 in English). References: '1 Corinthians 12:4-11' narrowed to 12:4-6 (12:11 is quoted separately); the Moses quotation, given only as Numbers 18:20, now cites Deuteronomy 18:1-2 first (the Levites named, 'the Lord is their portion') with Numbers 18:20; Deuteronomy 32:12 added for the opening words. Bracket filler 'the Holy [Spirit]' removed.

choices.term: οὐκ ἦν μετ' αὐτῶν θεὸς ἀλλότριος
choices.english: … there was no foreign god with them
choices.why: The section opens in the middle of Deuteronomy 32:12, begun in the previous section ('the Lord alone led them, and'); only these words are translated, with a leading ellipsis. ἀλλότριος here is 'foreign, alien', which Didymus glosses as 'of another substance'.
The adverb refers to Jude's letter as one of the catholic (general) epistles, not to a 'universal' manner of writing.

choices.term: ὡς κτήνη διὰ πεδίου κατέβη πνεῦμα παρὰ κυρίου
choices.english: like cattle through a plain, the Spirit came down from the Lord
choices.why: The copy-text runs the simile into the next clause without a stop; kept as one sentence. Didymus reads πνεῦμα as the Holy Spirit (his point in 19.16), so English uses 'the Spirit'.

choices.term: ἀπό τε τοῦ … ἀπό τε τοῦ παρακεῖσθαι
choices.english: first, because … and second, because beside them stands
choices.why: The double ἀπό τε gives the two grounds of 'overthrown twice over'; 'beside them stands' renders παρακεῖσθαι (the line lies next to these texts in Scripture).

choices.english: free and sovereign in his own right
choices.why: Didymus' term for the Spirit's own power of choice ('as he wills'); English needs a phrase, not a transliteration.
Standard sense of the word in 1 Corinthians 12; Pass A keeps 'distributions'.

choices.term: πισ τεύσαντας, Αἰγύπ του, ὡδήγη σεν, ἀλ λότριος, διακονι ῶν
choices.why: Words split by line breaks in the copy-text; read as single words.
The section ends on the colon that introduces a quotation in the next section; nothing from the next section is supplied. μέν anticipates a contrasting witness there.
